items.title: The Chattanooga Fire Department is teaming up with the National Fire Protection Association to support Fire Prevention W...
items.content_text:
The Chattanooga Fire Department is teaming up with the National Fire Protection Association to support Fire Prevention Week 2026. This year’s FPW theme, “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” focuses on the simple steps people can take to recharge safely. Safe charging means making smart choices every time you plug in.
 Many devices used in our daily lives - phones, tablets, laptops, tools, toys, e-bikes, and scooters—run on rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which store a lot of energy in a small space. If they are damaged or charged the wrong way, they can overheat, start a fire, or even explode.
 • Use the cord and charger that came with your device or one approved by the manufacturer. Using the wrong charger can damage the battery and increase the risk of fire.
 • Charge devices on a table, desk, or other hard, flat surface. Do not charge them on beds, couches, or under pillows. Devices and chargers produce heat during normal charging. Soft surfaces can trap heat and block airflow, which can cause the battery to overheat.
 • Stop using your device if it feels very hot, starts to swell, is smoking, or has a strange smell. These are warning signs that the battery may be damaged or failing.
 • Unplug your device when it is fully charged. Do not leave it plugged in longer than needed. Leaving a device plugged in too long can increase heat and stress on the battery.
 • Charge larger items like e-bikes, scooters, and power tools outside and away from exits. These batteries are larger and store more energy. If they fail, fires can grow quickly and spread. 
 • When on a plane, keep your device where you can see it while charging. Do not charge devices in overhead compartments. Do not charge e-cigarettes or vapes on a plane. If a battery overheats or fails, it is important for the flight crew to respond quickly.

items.content_text:
October is Pedestrian Safety Month, and the Tennessee Highway Safety Office is reminding both drivers and pedestrians to share the road responsibly:
 Drivers: Stay alert, put down distractions, and always yield to people in crosswalks.
 Pedestrians: Use sidewalks and marked crosswalks whenever available, make eye contact with drivers, and make sure you and your children are visible as it gets dark earlier.
 Stay safe this Fall!

Commercial fire response: On Sunday 10/04/26 at 4:38 AM, Green-shift companies responded to 2311 E 23rd St (Site Seven).
 Upon arrival crews found flames and smoke visible from the roof of the business. Command established water supply and aerial flow on the roof, while crews initiated interior attack on the main floor. The fire was quickly extinguished.
 No one was inside the business at the time of the incident.
 There were no injuries to CFD personnel.
 The cause is under investigation.
 Responding companies:
 Battalion 1, Battalion 2, Squad 13, Engine 1, Ladder 1, Squad 1, Engine 5, Ladder 5, Engine 9, CFD Supply, CFD Investigations

items.content_text:
Today, we celebrated a century of tradition, recreation and community at Brainerd Golf Course, and we couldn’t have asked for a better group to celebrate with, even with a little rain!
 Opened on October 3, 1926, Brainerd was designed by legendary golf architect Donald Ross and created with a simple vision: to provide quality, accessible outdoor recreation for the Chattanooga community.
 One hundred years later, that mission continues. Generations of golfers have made memories on these fairways, and Brainerd remains an important part of Chattanooga’s public golf tradition.
 Special shout out to Greta Hayes-Director of Recreation, Eddie Taylor-Director of Golf, Joe Starr-Director of Maintenance and Edwin Prichard-Brainerd Golf Manager. Combined, these individuals have over 115 years of service with City of Chattanooga golf. 
 Also thank you Mayor Kelly and District 5 Councilman Dennis Clark for sharing a few words. 
 A huge thank you to everyone who came out today, played in the 100 Year Celebration Two-Person Scramble, cheered on the players and helped us celebrate this incredible milestone.
 Here’s to 100 years of Brainerd Golf, and many more to come!

In 2024, bilateral donors and EU institutions mobilised USD 23.4 billion in private finance (commercial money channelled towards sustainable development objectives).
 But how was that money mobilised, and where was it invested?
 The 2026 #OECD Development Co-operation Profiles highlight how providers of development assistance are using public resources to attract private investment and which sectors are receiving support.
 Insights include how:
 ➡️ The United States mobilised USD 6.9 billion, followed by EU institutions (USD 6 billion) and Germany (USD 2.5 billion)
 ➡️ The banking and financial services sector accounted for more than one-third of all mobilised private finance
 ➡️ The energy sector represented 23% of the total
 ➡️ Together, banking and financial services and energy attracted more than half of all mobilised private finance in 2024.
 Find out more in the #DCprofiles2026: https://brnw.ch/21x68Gv
 #OECDdevelopment

items.title: Cuts in official development assistance (ODA) for health are concentrated in countries that rely most on external financ...
items.content_text:
Cuts in official development assistance (ODA) for health are concentrated in countries that rely most on external financing.
 ODA is financial support from governments promoting the economic development and welfare of developing countries.
 #OECD projections show that bilateral ODA for health could fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
 Some of the steepest reductions are expected in sub-Saharan Africa, where many countries rely on aid to support their health systems.
 ➡️ Uganda could see bilateral health ODA fall by 53.5% between 2024 and 2026.
 ➡️ Malawi and South Sudan could see declines of 50.8% and 42.4% respectively. External financing accounts for around 60% of current health expenditure in both countries.
 ➡️ Other recipient countries, including Mozambique and Lesotho, where external finance matters, are also projected to face significant reductions.
 Health is projected to experience the deepest cuts of any ODA sector between 2024 and 2026.
 For countries with limited fiscal space to replace declining support, these reductions could place additional pressure on already constrained health systems.
 Explore the latest data on ODA for health ➡️ https://brnw.ch/21x67Qi 
 #ODA2026 #OECDdevelopment

items.content_text:
Next up in our Exploring Downtown series: First Horizon Pavilion
 What is now an iconic venue for the Chattanooga Market, festivals, and gameday events was once a major industrial site. The Ross-Meehan Foundry operated for close to 100 years on Carter Street (now Reggie White Bouelvard), manufacturing various iron and steel castings for railway, automotive, military, and consumer use. In the 1920s and 1930s, the foundry even developed its own signature iron casting process, known as Meehanite. 
 In the mid-1980s, the Ross-Meehan Foundry would shut down and remain empty until 2003, when the structure was redeveloped into a 55,000 square foot open-air event space. Today, First Horizon Pavilion is a vibrant cultural hub, welcoming 350,000+ visitors annually. 
 Photo Credit: Steadfast Images | Matthew Roberts

items.title: 🚗💦 Where Does the Water Go After You Wash Your Car? Washing your car in your driveway may seem harmless, but the soapy...
items.content_text:
🚗💦 Where Does the Water Go After You Wash Your Car?
 Washing your car in your driveway may seem harmless, but the soapy water, dirt, oil, grease, and other pollutants don't go to a treatment plant. Instead, they flow into Red Bank's stormwater system, which is designed to quickly carry rainwater from our streets and neighborhoods directly to local waterways - like Stringers Branch.
 Unlike water that goes down your sink or toilet, stormwater receives little to no treatment before reaching our creeks and streams. That means anything washed off your vehicle can end up in the water that supports local wildlife and the health of our community.
 ✅ Consider using a commercial car wash, where wastewater is treated before being released, or washing your car in the grass in your yard.
 Only rain belongs in our storm drains! Protect our waterways and help keep Red Bank's aquatic ecosystems healthy.
 #RedBankTN #StormwaterMatters #ProtectOurStreams

Informal work, which isn't covered by national labour laws, is not taxed and does not provide access to worker protections such as pensions, remains the predominant form of employment worldwide, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, shaping the livelihoods of billions of workers and their families.  
 As populations age, technology transforms the world of work and environmental challenges increase, many informal workers are facing pressures such as limited pension protection, automation of work and vulnerability to climate risks. 
 What policies can help address this? 
 Find out at the launch of the #OECD report on Securing the Livelihoods of Informal Economy Workers in Times of Global Changes.

 Register now to attend online or in person ➡️ https://brnw.ch/21x6751

items.content_text:
Chattanooga Fire Department crews quickly contained a residential fire Thursday afternoon in the 4400 block of Drummond Drive.
 Green-shift companies arrived on scene to find smoke and flames coming from the front of the single-story residence. Crews quickly established water supply and conducted an interior search to confirm that no one remained inside. Firefighters then began an interior attack and quickly contained the fire.
 There were no injuries to CFD personnel or residents. However, two adults and two children were displaced as a result of the fire.
 The American Red Cross was called to provide assistance to the family.
 The cause is under investigation.
 Responding companies:
 Battalion 2, Battalion 3, Squad 13, Squad 1, Engine 10, Ladder 7, Engine 5, Engine 8, Squad 7, Ladder 5, Engine 4, Engine 6, Engine 15, CFD Investigations, HCEMS, CPD

Did you know? If you own property in #EastRidgeTN, but live outside the city limits, you may be eligible to vote in East Ridge municipal elections through Property Rights voting. 🗳️
 How to register:
 1. Confirm that you own property within the City of East Ridge.
 2. Contact the Hamilton County Election Commission. Ask about registering as an East Ridge Property Rights voter.
 3. Complete the required voter registration paperwork. The Election Commission will determine your eligibility and provide registration instructions.
 4. Register before the deadline. For the November 3, 2026 election, the voter registration deadline is Monday, October 5, 2026.
 5. Vote in the East Ridge municipal election. Property Rights voters are listed separately from the regular East Ridge precincts. Confirm voting instructions with the Election Commission.
 Questions about eligibility, documentation, or registration?
 📲 (423) 209-VOTE (8683)
 💻 https://elect.hamiltontn.gov
 Eligibility and registration requirements are determined by the Hamilton County Election Commission.

🏗️ DID YOU KNOW WHAT USED TO BE HERE?
 As the old grocery store and shopping center at 2101–2119 Dayton Boulevard are being cleared for new development, we thought it would be fun to take a little trip down memory lane. ❤️
 🛒 This spot has been a grocery store for generations of Red Bank families!
 📍 1970s: The shopping center was developed in the mid-1970s, and historical grocery records show Kroger operating at 2101 Dayton Blvd. by 1976.
 🛍️ Later years: The location became Save-A-Lot in early 2000s, serving Red Bank shoppers for many years before closing in 2022.
 And now, the building that so many people remember is coming down to make room for what's next for this corner of Red Bank.
 While the building may be gone soon, the memories aren't. ❤️
 Did you shop at the old Kroger, Red or Save-A-Lot?
 Maybe you remember a favorite cashier, something you always bought there, or even your first grocery trip as a kid.
 👇 Tell us what you remember! We'd love to hear some Red Bank memories from the community.

items.content_text:
It’s Throwback Thursday! With the Walnut Street Bridge reopening this Saturday, we’re looking back at another important reopening in the bridge’s history.
 Built in 1890, the Walnut Street Bridge originally carried horse-drawn wagons and pedestrians across the Tennessee River, and later, automobiles. After closing in 1978 due to structural concerns, the bridge sat unused for 15 years. Then, in 1993, it reopened with a new purpose: as a pedestrian-only bridge, thanks to a community effort to preserve this piece of Chattanooga history.
 More than three decades later, the Walnut Street Bridge remains a testament to that commitment to preservation and an important part of Chattanooga’s history, culture, and community. We’re excited to see it begin its next chapter this Saturday!

🎓 Congratulations, Kate Hackney! 🎓
 The City of Red Bank is proud to recognize our Executive Office Manager, Kate Hackney, on earning her Master Public Information Officer (PIO) Certification through the University of Tennessee Institute for Public Service! 🍊🏛️
 This POST-approved, multi-disciplinary certification provides advanced training for public information professionals in effectively communicating with the community and managing communications during both routine operations and times of crisis.
 Throughout the course, Kate expanded her knowledge and skills in:
 📣 Community engagement
 🎤 Advanced interviewing
 💡 Emotional intelligence
 🤝 Communicating in a multicultural community
 👩‍💼 Leading from your position
 🎥 Communicating an agency's mission through video
 🚨 Crisis communication strategies
 Participants also completed a group project focused on planning, writing, and delivering key messages — putting these skills into practice.
 One of the most valuable parts of the experience was the opportunity to connect and learn alongside public information and communications professionals from municipalities and public safety agencies across the state. Kate had the opportunity to network with professionals representing organizations including Metro Nashville Police Department, the City of Jackson, Bartlett Police Department, and the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, among others.
 Building these relationships and sharing ideas with other communities provides valuable perspectives that Kate can bring back to Red Bank as we continue to improve how we communicate with and serve our residents.
 As someone who plays an important role in keeping Red Bank residents informed and connected to their city, this certification is a wonderful reflection of Kate's continued commitment to professional development, effective communication, and public service.
 Please join us in congratulating Kate on this well-earned accomplishment! 👏🎓
 We are proud to have you representing the City of Red Bank, Kate! ❤️
 #CityOfRedBank #RedBankTN #MasterPIO #PublicInformationOfficer #PublicService #ProfessionalDevelopment #TeamRedBank #UTIPS

Did you know workforce development is part of what we do at SETD?

Through the Southeast Tennessee Local Workforce Development Board and American Job Center network, our workforce team helps connect people across our region with career pathways, training resources and employment opportunities.

Recently, Workforce Development Specialists Lauri Wilson and Raegan Russell joined students in grades 8–12 at the Meigs County High School College & Career Fair, where they talked with students about local employment opportunities, educational pathways, workforce programs and resources available as they begin thinking about their futures.

Workforce development plays an important role in creating opportunity across Southeast Tennessee. By connecting people with career resources, training and employment opportunities, our team is helping strengthen the region’s workforce and communities.

Strong communities start with strong opportunities for the people who call them home.

items.content_text:
Biodiversity underpins resilient economies, sustainable growth and human well-being. 
 New #OECD analysis estimates global biodiversity finance at USD 74.9-92.4 billion per year (2023-25 average). 
 Key findings include:
 ➡️ Public domestic expenditure remains the largest source of biodiversity finance, accounting for around two-thirds of total funding.
 ➡️ Biodiversity finance is on the rise: international public finance grew by 94% between 2018-20 and 2023-24, and private finance by 73% between 2018-20 and 2023-25.
 ➡️ Better biodiversity finance data can help accelerate action, enabling governments and investors to track progress, identify gaps and direct resources where they can have the greatest impact. 
 Find out more: https://brnw.ch/21x65EC

UTC’s acquisition of the Doctors Building in 2000 marked an important moment in the growth of campus. Located at the southwest corner of McCallie Avenue and Palmetto Street, the real estate purchase marked the University’s first expansion south across McCallie Avenue.
 Planned in 1955 by Atlanta-based realtor Sam Massell Jr., the structure was originally a professional office building for physicians, surgeons, dentists and other healthcare providers. Interior spaces were outfitted with laboratory gas lines, exhaust fans, heavy-duty X-ray wiring and configured for the “Music by Muzak” system.
 🔗  Learn more here: https://blog.utc.edu/…/if-these-walls-could-talk-doctors-b…/
